title: Freight Forwarder Digital Transformation: A Practical Roadmap for 2026
summary: Discover how freight forwarders are modernizing operations through automation, visibility, and AI. Learn practical strategies to reduce manual work and scale efficiently.
body_text: Freight forwarding has always been operationally complex. But in 2026, the gap between forwarders running on manual workflows and those using automation is widening fast. Customers now expect faster quotes, real-time shipment visibility, and proactive communication, all with fewer operational delays. Meanwhile, many forwarding teams are still juggling spreadsheets, emails and disconnected systems across every shipment. That’s why digital transformation has become less about “innovation” and more about operational survival. Key Takeaways Freight forwarder digital transformation focuses on automating workflows , improving visibility, and reducing operational inefficiencies. Workflow fragmentation, not lack of software, is often the biggest operational bottleneck. Fast quoting and proactive communication have become major competitive advantages. Real-time shipment visibility is now a baseline expectation for many shippers. AI adoption in freight forwarding is becoming practical, especially around pricing, forecasting, and operational analysis. The most successful modernization projects happen incrementally, not through massive system overhauls. Why Freight Forwarder Digital Transformation Became Urgent For years, digital transformation in freight forwarding was treated as a future initiative rather than an immediate operational priority. What changed was customer expectation. Digital-native logistics companies reset the standard for responsiveness, visibility, and customer experience. Real-time tracking, instant quotes, and proactive notifications no longer feel like premium features. Many shippers now expect them by default. At the same time, operational pressure inside freight forwarding businesses has intensified as margins tighten and customers expect faster service. Yet many forwarders still rely heavily on spreadsheets, inboxes, PDFs, and disconnected systems. The result is operational drag: duplicate data, delayed statuses, and fragmented documentation with errors. The forwarders gaining market share today are often not the largest companies. They are the ones operating more efficiently. Why It Matters: Digital transformation is no longer about experimenting with new technology. It is increasingly about removing operational friction before competitors do. The Real Bottleneck Is Workflow Fragmentation One of the biggest misconceptions about freight forwarder digital transformation is that companies need to replace every system they already use. In reality, most operational problems come from disconnected workflows. The issue is that freight forwarders use many systems that rarely communicate cleanly with one another. As a result, operations teams become the integration layer between systems. Shipment data gets copied across platforms manually. Documents move through email threads. Status updates depend on employees checking carrier portals and refreshing milestones manually. Individually, these tasks seem manageable. At scale, they create major inefficiencies. The goal of digital transformation is not to replace operational expertise. It is to remove repetitive administrative work surrounding that expertise. The freight forwarders operating most efficiently today are usually running coherent workflows: connected systems centralized operational data automated updates integrated quoting and tracking fewer manual handoffs That operational consistency becomes a commercial advantage because customers feel the difference immediately. Why It Matters: Most freight forwarders do not need more software. They need fewer disconnected workflows. Why Quoting Is Often the First Workflow to Automate Freight quoting remains one of the most manual workflows in logistics. A typical process still involves: Checking carrier rate sheets Reviewing market pricing Calculating margins manually Formatting quotes Emailing revisions back and forth Meanwhile, customers are often requesting quotes from multiple providers simultaneously. By the time many forwarders respond, the customer has already narrowed the field. This is why quoting automation is often one of the first investments in digital transformation. However, effective quote automation typically starts before the quote itself. Forwarders first need accurate, up-to-date pricing data. Without a reliable process for collecting and maintaining carrier rates, even the best quoting workflows will struggle to deliver accurate results. Once that foundation is in place, modern quoting systems can connect directly to carrier pricing sources, apply margin rules automatically, generate customer-ready quotes in seconds, and standardize pricing workflows. The benefits extend beyond operational efficiency. In freight forwarding, responsiveness signals reliability. Faster quoting helps improve customer experience while allowing teams to spend less time on administrative work and more time on strategic accounts, exception management, and customer relationships. Why It Matters: Quoting is often the first step in the customer lifecycle. Building the right pricing and data foundation not only improves responsiveness, but also creates opportunities to automate and streamline workflows throughout the rest of the operation. Visibility Has Become a Baseline Expectation One of the most common customer questions in freight forwarding is still: "Where is my shipment?" Without centralized visibility tools, operations teams often spend significant time responding to status requests, checking carrier portals, and manually communicating shipment updates. That is why real-time shipment visibility has become one of the defining pillars of freight forwarder digital transformation. Modern visibility platforms allow milestone updates to flow automatically from carriers, ports, customs systems, warehouses, and delivery events. Instead of chasing updates manually, customers receive shipment information proactively. The operational benefits are immediate: Fewer repetitive inquiries Faster exception management Reduced email volume Improved customer experience Visibility is also becoming a commercial requirement. Many enterprise shippers now expect customer portals, proactive notifications, real-time tracking, and self-service shipment visibility as part of the standard service experience. Forwarders that lack these capabilities increasingly struggle to compete for larger accounts. Why It Matters: Shipment visibility is no longer a premium feature. For many shippers, it's a baseline expectation and a key factor in evaluating logistics partners. Documentation and Compliance Challenges Freight forwarding still depends heavily on documentation accuracy. Bills of lading, customs filings, invoices, packing lists, and compliance records move across multiple systems and stakeholders throughout the shipment lifecycle. When documentation workflows remain manual, small errors can quickly become costly. Common issues include: Customs delays Filing penalties Invoice discrepancies Shipment holds Prolonged dispute resolution Digital documentation workflows help reduce these risks by centralizing records, automating validation checks, maintaining version control, and improving auditability. Why It Matters: Documentation may not be the most visible part of freight forwarding, but it is one of the most operationally critical. Centralized workflows help reduce risk, improve accuracy, and keep shipments moving efficiently. AI in Freight Forwarding Is Becoming Practical For years, discussions about AI in logistics felt largely theoretical. Today, that is starting to change as freight forwarders find practical ways to apply AI across their operations. McKinsey notes that advances in AI could reshape how freight and logistics companies manage planning, execution, and operational decision-making. The most valuable applications in freight forwarding are not focused on replacing operators. They help teams make faster decisions using data they already have, including shipment history, lane profitability, carrier performance, transit consistency, and customer behavior patterns. Today, AI-powered systems can help teams: Optimize pricing decisions Identify margin leakage Forecast operational bottlenecks Evaluate carrier reliability Analyze shipment trends The forwarders seeing the greatest impact from AI are usually not building custom machine-learning infrastructure themselves. They are using operational data more effectively to improve performance and make better decisions. Why It Matters: The competitive advantage isn't AI itself. It's the ability to turn operational data into faster decisions, better customer experiences, and more profitable operations. What Most Freight Forwarders Get Wrong About Digital Transformation One of the most common mistakes freight forwarders make is treating digital transformation like a massive one-time overhaul. That approach rarely works. The most successful modernization efforts usually happen incrementally, starting with one high-friction workflow at a time: Quoting Shipment visibility Documentation Invoicing Customs workflows This sequencing matters because adoption matters. Many failed digital transformation projects are not really technology failures. They are change-management failures. Teams resist new systems when the tools create more friction before they create value. The forwarders that modernize successfully usually start with immediately painful operational problems: reducing repetitive work, eliminating duplicate data entry, minimizing email dependency, improving visibility, and simplifying coordination. Once teams experience clear operational improvements, adoption becomes much easier. Why It Matters: The goal is not to reinvent freight forwarding operations overnight. It is to reduce dependency on manual coordination one workflow at a time. Summary Freight forwarding has always been operationally demanding. What is changing is the speed, visibility, and efficiency customers now expect from logistics providers. Disconnected workflows have become increasingly expensive to maintain at scale. The freight forwarders gaining an advantage today are usually not the ones adopting the most software. They are the ones building operational consistency: automating repetitive work connecting systems cleanly improving visibility reducing manual coordination enabling teams to scale more efficiently Over time, those operational improvements compound into commercial advantages. Frequently Asked Questions What is freight forwarder digital transformation? Freight forwarder digital transformation refers to the use of automation, integrations, AI, and centralized operational systems to modernize freight operations, reduce manual workflows, and improve shipment visibility. Why is digital transformation important in freight forwarding? Digital transformation helps freight forwarders improve response times, automate repetitive tasks, reduce operational errors, and meet growing customer expectations around visibility and communication. What processes can freight forwarders automate? Common automation areas include: freight quoting shipment tracking document management customs workflows invoicing customer notifications carrier rate management How is AI used in freight forwarding? AI is increasingly used for: pricing optimization carrier performance analysis operational forecasting margin analysis workflow automation exception management What are the biggest challenges in freight forwarder digital transformation? The biggest challenges are usually: disconnected legacy systems manual workflows change management poor system integrations operational resistance to new processes ‍ Reform helps freight forwarders , customs brokers , shippers , and carriers automate critical workflows without replacing the systems they already rely on. From quoting and booking to documentation and shipment operations, Reform reduces manual overhead, improves response times, and helps teams scale with less complexity.

title: Bone Spurs: Symptoms, Causes, Treatment and Relief
summary: Bone spurs, or osteophytes, can cause pain, stiffness, and limited movement. Learn the symptoms, causes, and treatment options, including nonsurgical care
body_text: Nearly one in three adults over the age of 60 has a bone spur, even if they don’t know it. These bony overgrowths, called osteophytes, are among the most common age-related changes in the body—and while many go unnoticed, others can cause chronic pain, joint stiffness, or nerve irritation that affects daily life. You may not realize you have a bone spur until it begins to interfere with your activities. For some people, symptoms begin with heel pain that flares up in the morning. For others, it may be stiffness in the neck, a loss of flexibility in the shoulder, or tingling in the fingers. These issues may seem unrelated, but they often stem from the same underlying problem: excessive bone formation near a joint under stress. Bone spurs are a natural part of the body’s response to wear and tear, but that doesn’t mean they are always harmless. Depending on where they form and the amount of pressure they create, they can limit movement, irritate soft tissue, or compress nearby nerves. This guide explores what bone spurs are, why they develop, who is most at risk, and how to find relief with conservative care. What are bone spurs? Bone spurs are smooth, hard bumps of extra bone that form along the edges of bones, usually where bones meet at joints. This process, called osteophyte formation, is your body’s way of protecting a joint that is under stress or experiencing instability. Despite the name, bone spurs do not look like spikes. They often develop slowly and may not cause problems until they press on nearby nerves, restrict movement, or aggravate surrounding tissue. Bone spurs can form in many areas of the body, including the spine, shoulders, hips, knees, feet, and hands. They are common in adults over the age of 50 but may occur earlier, especially in athletes or individuals with repetitive joint stress. What causes bone spurs? Bone spurs form as your body’s way of protecting a joint under stress. When joints experience ongoing pressure, friction, or instability, the body may begin to produce extra bone in an attempt to reinforce the area. This process is unrelated to dietary calcium or supplements. Instead, it is your body’s natural response to wear and tear. Here are some of the most common causes of bone spur development and how they contribute: Osteoarthritis When cartilage begins to wear away due to age or joint degeneration, bones lose the smooth padding that allows them to glide easily. In response, the body tries to stabilize the joint by forming new bone along the edges. These growths often occur where two bones meet and are a hallmark of advanced osteoarthritis . Tendon or ligament inflammation Inflammation from conditions like plantar fasciitis or Achilles tendinitis places repeated tension on the area where soft tissues attach to bone. Over time, this chronic pulling may lead the body to build up extra bone at the attachment site, which is how heel spurs and other similar bony projections form. Degenerative disc disease As spinal discs lose height and hydration, they become less effective at cushioning the vertebrae. To stabilize the spine and reduce movement between vertebrae, the body may produce bone spurs around the disc space. These may eventually contribute to stiffness or nerve compression in the spine. Postural stress or repetitive motion Poor posture, repetitive tasks, or uneven joint loading can increase stress on specific areas of the body. This constant mechanical pressure signals the body to adapt. Over time, it may do so by building up bone near affected joints, particularly in the neck, shoulders, hips, or feet. Previous injury or trauma A fracture, sprain, or dislocation can change the way a joint functions. To restore stability and protect the area, the body may create new bone along the affected joint. Scar tissue, joint laxity, and altered movement patterns all contribute to spur development after injury. Bone spurs don’t appear overnight. They form slowly in response to chronic stress or imbalance in the body. While this is a protective mechanism, the result can sometimes cause more harm than good, especially if the new bone growth interferes with nerves, limits mobility, or contributes to joint pain. Understanding the underlying cause is the first step toward managing symptoms and preventing future problems. Where in your body do bone spurs commonly occur? Bone spurs can form anywhere in the body where repeated pressure, joint friction, or soft tissue stress occurs. They typically appear near joints or where tendons and ligaments anchor to bone. While they may not always cause symptoms, certain locations are more likely to create discomfort or movement limitations. Here are some of the most common areas affected by bone spurs and how they develop: Spine Bone spurs frequently develop in the cervical (neck) and lumbar (lower back) regions of the spine. They often form in response to disc degeneration or chronic spinal instability. As the discs between vertebrae shrink or lose structure, the spine creates extra bone to protect itself. These spurs may narrow the spaces where nerves exit the spine, potentially causing pain, numbness, or tingling that radiates into the arms or legs. Shoulders In the shoulder, bone spurs may form on the underside of the acromion or near the rotator cuff. This often results from chronic inflammation, overuse, or age-related degeneration. As tendons move under the acromion, spurs may cause impingement, making it painful to lift the arm overhead or reach behind the back. Over time, this may lead to reduced mobility and chronic shoulder dysfunction. Hips Bone spurs in the hip joint usually develop in response to osteoarthritis, repetitive impact, or previous injury. As cartilage wears down and joint movement becomes less smooth, the body creates extra bone to reinforce the joint. This may lead to stiffness in the groin or outer hip and can cause pain while walking, climbing stairs, or sitting for extended periods. Knees In the knees, bone spurs often appear along the edges of the joint in people with arthritis. As the joint surface deteriorates, spurs form in an attempt to improve stability. These growths may limit the range of motion and cause pain during activities that involve bending, squatting, or prolonged standing. They may also contribute to joint stiffness or a sensation of grinding during movement. Feet and heels Heel spurs are among the most well-known types of bone spurs and typically form at the base of the heel bone. They often develop where the plantar fascia connects to the heel, which is a thick band of tissue that supports the arch of the foot. Repeated strain from walking, standing, or wearing unsupportive footwear may irritate this area and trigger new bone growth. Heel spurs do not always cause pain, but when they do, the discomfort is often sharp and most noticeable with the first steps of the morning. Hands and Fingers Bone spurs in the fingers and hands are common with age-related joint degeneration, especially osteoarthritis. These spurs often develop at the ends of the finger joints and may appear as small, hard lumps. While they are not always painful, they may reduce flexibility, affect grip strength, or make fine motor tasks more difficult. Bone spurs can appear anywhere in the body where it responds to long-term stress or inflammation. Their impact depends on their location, size, and whether they interfere with nerves, joints, or surrounding soft tissues. Recognizing where they occur and how they affect the body is a key step in finding effective relief. Who is at risk for developing bone spurs? Bone spurs can affect people of all ages, but they are significantly more common in adults over 50. According to population studies, osteophytes are one of the most frequent age-related changes in the musculoskeletal system. Imaging studies suggest that the majority of adults over 60 have at least one bone spur, even if they do not have symptoms. While bone spurs can form in response to specific joint stress or injury, certain individuals are more likely to develop them due to lifestyle, health conditions, and anatomical factors. The most common risk factors include: Older adults The risk of developing bone spurs increases with age. Over time, joints experience more wear and tear, which makes it more likely for the body to respond by creating extra bone. People over 50 are much more likely to develop osteophytes, especially in the spine, hips, knees, and hands. People with osteoarthritis Bone spurs often appear alongside joint degeneration. As cartilage wears away, the body may attempt to stabilize the joint by building new bone. Nearly all adults with moderate to severe osteoarthritis will have bone spurs near affected joints. Physically active individuals Athletes and people with physically demanding jobs are more likely to experience repetitive joint stress. High-impact movement, heavy lifting, and repetitive overuse can all increase the likelihood of bone spur formation in weight-bearing joints, such as the knees, hips, or spine. People with poor posture or spinal misalignment Chronic postural strain places uneven pressure on the spine and other joints, resulting in strain. Over time, this may lead to compensatory bone growth, particularly in the neck and lower back. Individuals with previous joint injuries A history of fractures, dislocations, or joint trauma may disrupt normal biomechanics. This may lead the body to adapt by producing new bone to reinforce the joint, even years after the original injury. People with excess body weight Carrying extra body weight increases the mechanical load on weight-bearing joints, especially in the lower back, hips, knees, and feet. This added stress may accelerate joint degeneration and lead to the formation of bone spurs over time. Studies show that individuals with a body mass index (BMI) of 30 or higher are significantly more likely to develop osteophytes, particularly in the knees and spine. Each unit increase in BMI is associated with a measurable increase in joint stress and a higher risk of both osteoarthritis and associated bony growths. Genetic predisposition Some people may inherit structural traits or inflammatory tendencies that increase the risk of both arthritis and bone spur formation. If osteoarthritis runs in your family, you may be more likely to develop related joint changes. People with abnormal foot mechanics Flat feet, high arches, or poor-quality footwear may increase stress on the heels and ankles. These structural issues may raise the risk of developing heel spurs and other bone growths in the feet. Bone spurs are extremely common, especially later in life. While not all spurs cause symptoms, paying attention to joint health and mobility as you age may help reduce your risk and support long-term function. Regular movement, proper posture, and early care for joint discomfort may help you avoid complications before they begin. Symptoms of bone spurs: What do they feel like? Not all bone spurs cause symptoms. In many cases, they are discovered by accident during an X-ray or MRI for an unrelated issue. But when symptoms do appear, they are often a sign that the spur is interfering with nearby tissue, pressing on a nerve, or affecting joint movement. If a bone spur is causing symptoms, you may experience one or more of the following: Localized joint pain: Pain is the most common symptom and may feel sharp, dull, or achy depending on the location. It often flares during movement or physical activity and eases with rest. For example, a bone spur in the shoulder may cause pain when lifting your arm, while one in the spine may cause pain with bending, twisting, or prolonged standing. Joint stiffness or reduced range of motion: Bone spurs can limit the joint's ability to move, making everyday motions feel tight or restricted. You might notice that your neck no longer turns as easily, or that your knees feel stiff after sitting. This stiffness can be especially noticeable in the morning or after periods of inactivity. Numbness or tingling: If a bone spur presses on a nearby nerve, it may lead to numbness, tingling, or a “pins and needles” sensation. These symptoms are more common in the spine, particularly in the neck or lower back, and may radiate into the arms, hands, legs, or feet. In some cases, nerve compression may also cause weakness or coordination issues. Swelling or tenderness: Bone spurs may irritate surrounding soft tissue, including tendons and ligaments. This may result in inflammation, localized swelling, or tenderness to the touch. For instance, a heel spur may cause a sore, inflamed spot at the bottom of the foot, especially after prolonged walking or standing. Joint locking, clicking, or catching: When a bone spur disrupts the smooth movement of a joint, you may feel or hear a clicking or grinding sensation during motion. Some people describe the joint as feeling like it is “catching” or locking temporarily before releasing again. This is most common in joints like the knee, shoulder, or fingers. The way bone spurs feel depends on their size, shape, and location, as well as the extent to which they interfere with nearby structures. Some people experience only mild discomfort, while others may struggle with daily movement or chronic pain. If symptoms persist or worsen, it may be a sign that the spur is affecting your nerve or joint function and requires evaluation. Are bone spurs dangerous? Bone spurs themselves are not inherently dangerous. Many people have them without any symptoms or complications. However, problems can arise if a bone spur: Presses on a nerve or spinal cord, leading to pain, numbness, or weakness Restricts joint movement and function Causes chronic irritation or inflammation in nearby tissue If you experience persistent pain, reduced mobility, or signs of nerve involvement, it is essential to seek medical care. Identifying and addressing the underlying cause may prevent further damage and improve your quality of life. How are bone spurs diagnosed? Diagnosing a bone spur typically begins with a thorough clinical evaluation. A healthcare provider will ask about your symptoms, medical history, activity level, and any previous joint injuries. During the physical exam, they will assess for tenderness around joints, swelling, limitations in range of motion, and signs of nerve involvement, such as numbness, tingling, or weakness. If a bone spur is suspected, imaging tests are usually recommended to confirm the diagnosis and assess the surrounding structures. These may include: X-rays X-rays are the most common starting point. They provide a clear view of bone structure and can reveal the presence, size, and location of a bone spur. X-rays also help identify signs of joint degeneration, such as cartilage loss or narrowing of the joint space, which often accompany osteophyte formation. MRI or CT scans Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and computed tomography (CT) scans offer more detailed views of the soft tissues surrounding a joint. These tests are especially useful when symptoms suggest nerve compression, such as radiating pain or muscle weakness. An MRI can reveal whether a bone spur is pressing on a nerve, tendon, or spinal cord, while CT scans provide a high-resolution view of complex joints, such as the spine, hips, or shoulders. Nerve conduction studies When bone spurs are suspected of affecting nerve function, nerve conduction velocity (NCV) tests and electromyography (EMG) may be used to assess nerve function. These tests measure how well electrical signals travel through the nerves and muscles. They can detect nerve compression or damage caused by a spur in the neck, lower back, or extremities, helping to guide treatment and assess severity. Additional evaluations In some cases, your provider may recommend joint aspiration, blood work, or referral to a specialist to rule out other conditions, especially if your symptoms involve widespread joint pain, inflammation, or systemic issues. A clear and accurate diagnosis is essential for creating an effective treatment plan. Once your provider identifies the presence and impact of a bone spur, they can recommend appropriate care to manage symptoms, restore function, and prevent further complications. Treatment options for bone spurs Treatment for bone spurs depends on several factors, including their size, location, and the extent to which they affect surrounding structures. Many people find relief without surgery, especially when symptoms are mild to moderate. The goal of treatment is to reduce pain, improve function, and prevent the spur from interfering with daily life. In most cases, providers begin with conservative, nonsurgical options before considering more invasive procedures. Nonsurgical options for treating bone spurs Chiropractic care Gentle spinal or joint adjustments may help restore alignment, reduce pressure on irritated tissues, and improve overall joint function. For bone spurs in the spine, chiropractic care may also relieve associated nerve compression symptoms, such as radiating pain or numbness. This hands-on approach supports better mobility and may help reduce stiffness caused by mechanical stress. Physical therapy A personalized physical therapy program focuses on restoring joint strength, balance, and flexibility. Therapists may guide you through exercises that improve posture, reduce joint strain, and correct movement patterns that contribute to pain. Over time, this can help you move more comfortably and lower the risk of further irritation. Massage therapy Soft tissue therapy helps reduce muscle tightness and improve circulation around affected joints. This may be especially helpful when nearby muscles have become tense or inflamed in response to the bone spur. By relaxing the surrounding tissue, massage may help ease discomfort and support more fluid movement. Stretching and mobility routines Daily stretching may help maintain the range of motion in joints affected by bone spurs. These routines promote joint flexibility, reduce stiffness, and improve body mechanics. For many people, consistent mobility work is key to preventing further joint restriction. Ice or heat therapy Cold therapy may be useful for reducing inflammation after activity or during a flare-up, while heat may help relax stiff muscles and improve circulation before movement. Alternating the two may offer additional relief, depending on your symptoms. Over-the-counter pain relievers Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), such as ibuprofen or naproxen, may help manage pain and swelling. These are typically used during symptom flare-ups or after physical activity that aggravates the joint. Supportive devices Orthotics, braces, or ergonomic supports may relieve pressure on affected joints and improve body alignment. For example, custom shoe inserts may help reduce heel spur pain, while lumbar supports may provide relief for bone spurs in the lower back. These nonsurgical approaches are often enough to manage bone spur symptoms and allow you to remain active. With consistency, many people find that their pain levels decrease and their joint function improves. When to consider surgery for bone spurs Surgery is typically considered only when other treatments have not worked or when the bone spur is causing significant impairment. While not all bone spurs require surgical intervention, it may be the best option in certain cases. Surgery may be recommended if: Conservative treatments have failed to relieve pain or improve function A bone spur is pressing on a nerve and causing weakness, numbness, or radiating pain The spur is interfering with the normal movement or structural integrity of the joint You are preparing for a joint replacement or other orthopedic procedure, and the spur would limit success Surgical options vary by location and severity but may include: Bone spur removal to eliminate the excess bone and reduce pressure on surrounding tissues Surgical spinal decompression procedures to relieve nerve compression in the spine caused by osteophytes Joint replacement in cases where arthritis and bone spur formation have severely damaged the joint Recovery from surgery depends on the specific procedure, your overall health status, and the intensity of your rehabilitation efforts. In many cases, physical therapy is needed after surgery to restore mobility and function. Surgery is not right for everyone, but when appropriate, it can provide meaningful relief and improve long-term outcomes for people with severe or persistent bone spur complications. Can a chiropractor help with bone spurs? Chiropractors do not remove bone spurs, but they may play a valuable role in relieving the symptoms these bony growths cause. When a bone spur develops near a joint, particularly in the spine, it may disrupt alignment, limit mobility, and place added stress on surrounding muscles and nerves. This often leads to compensatory tension, changes in movement patterns, and ongoing discomfort. Chiropractic care focuses on restoring healthy joint mechanics and relieving the pressure that exacerbates bone spur symptoms. Rather than treating the spur itself, chiropractors address the structural imbalances and soft tissue stress that allow symptoms to persist or worsen. Chiropractic care may help treat bone spurs by: Improving joint alignment and mobility Adjustments may help restore proper joint motion, especially when stiffness or muscle guarding is present. This is particularly important in the spine, where bone spurs often develop in areas affected by disc degeneration or poor posture. By enhancing joint movement, chiropractic care may reduce mechanical irritation caused by the spur and support better spinal function. Reducing muscle tension and inflammation Chronic joint dysfunction may cause the surrounding muscles to tighten, helping to stabilize the area. Over time, this leads to discomfort, fatigue, and limited range of motion. Chiropractic adjustments, combined with soft tissue techniques, may help relax these muscles and enhance circulation to the affected area. Supporting posture and movement patterns When bone spurs affect your biomechanics, it can lead to compensations throughout the body. Chiropractic care may help identify and correct these patterns by improving alignment and reducing asymmetry, thereby preventing further stress on the affected joint. Relieving pressure on nerves and nearby structures In the spine, even small bone spurs can narrow the spaces where nerves exit, a condition known as foraminal stenosis. While chiropractic care does not remove the spur, adjustments may help reduce joint inflammation or disc pressure, which in turn may ease nerve irritation and improve overall comfort. Chiropractic is part of a broader care plan for bone spurs Chiropractic care is often most effective when paired with other conservative therapies, such as stretching, targeted exercises, ergonomic adjustments, and massage. This collaborative approach may help restore joint function, improve flexibility, and keep you active without the need for invasive treatment. For many people, regular chiropractic care is a proactive approach to managing bone spur symptoms, maintaining mobility, and supporting long-term joint health. If you are experiencing stiffness, discomfort, or nerve-related symptoms associated with bone spurs, a chiropractor can assess your condition and provide personalized strategies for relief. Final thoughts: Living with bone spurs Bone spurs are common, especially as we age or experience long-term joint stress. While they can sound alarming, they often cause little to no symptoms and are manageable with the right care. Whether you are dealing with discomfort in your heel, stiffness in your spine, or tingling in your fingers, there are options available to help you feel better and move more freely. By addressing the underlying cause and working with a trusted provider, you can maintain your activity level, alleviate pain, and take control of your long-term joint health. Frequently asked questions about bone spurs Do bone spurs go away? No. Bone spurs do not disappear on their own, but their symptoms can often be managed with proper care. Are bone spurs always painful? No. Many bone spurs cause no symptoms and are found incidentally on X-rays. Is a heel spur the same as a bone spur? A heel spur is a type of bone spur located at the bottom of the heel, often associated with plantar fasciitis. Can bone spurs be treated without surgery? Most people find relief with nonsurgical care such as chiropractic adjustments, physical therapy, and home remedies. Is a bone spur caused by too much calcium? Bone spurs result from joint stress and degeneration, not from dietary calcium. title: GoldMining Commences 2026 Exploration Drilling Program at its Yarumalito Gold-Copper Project, Colombia
summary: GoldMining Inc. is a public mineral exploration company advancing gold-copper projects in the Americas through exploration, strategic investments, and partnerships.
body_text: GoldMining Commences 2026 Exploration Drilling Program at its Yarumalito Gold-Copper Project, Colombia Share: Vancouver, British Columbia – May 26, 2026 – GoldMining Inc. (TSX: GOLD; NYSE American: GLDG) (the "Company" or "GoldMining") is pleased to announce that it has commenced an exploration-focused core drilling program on its 100%-owned Yarumalito Gold-Copper Project ("Yarumalito" or the "Project") in the Mid Cauca gold-copper belt of Antioquia, Colombia. Highlights: Fully Funded Drill Program Underway: The diamond core drill is actively turning on site for an approximate 1,200-metre systematic program. Testing a New and Enhanced Geological Model: Drilling will follow-up on high priority targets previously identified through comprehensive relogging of historical core. Expanding the Mineralized P-1 Porphyry: Testing new zones of potential bedrock mineralization in under-drilled portions of the host ‘P-1’ porphyry unit, the principal host of gold-copper (“Au-Cu”) mineralization at the Project. Building on Historical Drill Intercepts : 257 metres ("m") at 0.50 grams per tonne ("g/t") gold ("Au") and 0.1% copper (“Cu”) from surface (YAR-06) 250 m at 0.51 g/t Au and 0.13% Cu from surface (YAR-08) 141.4 m at 0.77 g/t Au and 0.09% Cu from surface (YAR-11) Alastair Still, President and Chief Executive Officer of GoldMining, commented: “Yarumalito sits in the heart of Colombia’s prolific Mid Cauca belt, in close proximity to major discoveries like Collective Mining’s Guayabales project and Aris Mining’s Marmato mine. With diamond core drilling now underway on our second active exploration drilling program in the Americas for 2026, we are testing a newly refined geological model at Yarumalito. This large, highly accessible gold-copper porphyry system remains open in all directions and the targeted drill program is our first step in seeking to unlock the substantial step-out growth potential of the mineralized P-1 host unit.” About Yarumalito The 100% owned Yarumalito project is located in the Mid Cauca Au-Cu Belt of central Colombia, approximately 105 kilometers south-southwest of Medellín, Colombia’s second most important economic center, and 40 kilometers south of the Company’s La Mina project. Neighbouring projects include Aris Mining Corporation’s Marmato Gold Mine and Collective Mining Ltd.’s Guayabales Project. Gold-copper mineralization is related to porphyry intrusive bodies of potassic altered diorite with disseminated and fracture-controlled pyrite, chalcopyrite and magnetic, which is cross-cut by structurally controlled intermediate sulphidation epithermal veins containing pyrite, galena, sphalerite and chalcopyrite. An existing mineral resource estimate ("MRE") was previously completed by the Company on the Project based on 50 historical drill holes (drilled between 2005 and 2013) containing approximately 18,000 m of core. The MRE comprises 66.3 million tonnes at 0.58 g/t Au and 0.09% Cu for 1.23 million ounces Au and 129 million pounds Cu of estimated inferred mineral resources. For further information regarding the Project, including the MRE, please see the ‘ Technical Report Yarumalito Gold-Copper Property, Departments of Antioquia and Caldas, Republic of Colombia ’, with an effective date of April 1, 2020, a copy of which is available under the Company’s profile on SEDAR+ at www.sedarplus.ca . The approximate 1,200 m planned core drilling program is expected to comprise three drill holes to test the geometry and extents of the porphyry-style of mineralization in the ‘P-1’ intrusive phase, which is demonstrated from systematic relogging of historical drill core to represent the principal host lithology of the gold and copper mineralization. A fourth drill hole is planned to target epithermal veins mapped from abandoned underground historical mine workings, with the objective to test the geometry, width and grade characteristics of the over-printing epithermal mineralization. The minor underground historic workings are not active and there is no known artisanal mining occurring on the Property. Figure1 Location map of Yarumalito Project in the Mid Cauca Au-Cu Belt of central Colombia. title: 6 Best Access Management Tools for SOC 2 Compliance in 2026
summary: Compare the 6 best access management tools for SOC 2 compliance in 2026. Find solutions that automate provisioning and reviews without SCIM.
body_text: Most access management tools solve SOC 2 compliance by making you upgrade your entire SaaS stack to enterprise pricing tiers just to support SCIM and SAML integrations. If you're a Series A to Series C company with 40+ applications and one IT hire, that approach breaks your budget before it solves your audit problem. We tested access management tools for SOC 2 to identify which ones automate the full access lifecycle across your actual SaaS environment, including the long tail of smaller apps your vendors want you to pay more for. TLDR: Access management tools automate provisioning, approvals, and reviews to meet SOC 2 requirements Most tools require SCIM/SAML, forcing expensive SaaS upgrades across your entire stack Access reviews should remediate issues immediately, not weeks after discovery Shadow IT detection surfaces unauthorized apps that create compliance blind spots AccessOwl automates access governance without enterprise prerequisites or long deployments What Are Access Management Tools for SOC 2 Compliance? Access management tools for SOC 2 compliance help you govern, automate, and audit user interactions with your SaaS applications. They exist to answer what your auditor will ask: who has access to what, and can you prove it? SOC 2 examinations focus on controls relevant to security, availability, and confidentiality. Your organization needs to show evidence of: Role-based access controls that match job functions to appropriate permission levels across every application in your stack Formal provisioning and deprovisioning tied to the employee lifecycle, from day-one onboarding through offboarding Periodic access reviews to verify that permissions are still appropriate and haven't drifted over time Approval workflows with a clear audit trail showing who requested access, who approved it, and when Timely revocation when someone changes roles or leaves the company, with documented proof of removal For a Series A or Series B company with a small IT team, managing this in spreadsheets gets painful fast. The best access management tools handle the full governance lifecycle: detecting Shadow IT, automating account creation and removal , routing approval requests, and generating compliance evidence without manual effort . If you can't show an auditor a clean trail from access request to approval to periodic review, your SOC 2 readiness has a gap, no matter how good your security posture looks on paper. How We Ranked These Access Management Tools We built our evaluation criteria around the reality most Series A to Series C companies face: lean teams, tight timelines, and auditors who won't care about your resource constraints. Here's what we weighted: Integration breadth: Can it handle apps your team actually uses beyond the big-name ones? Automation without enterprise prerequisites: Many tools require SCIM or SAML , which are locked behind expensive enterprise tiers. We favored tools that automate lifecycle management through APIs, service accounts, or RPA. Access review workflows: We tested review setup, remediation speed, and evidence export. Tools requiring spreadsheets scored lower. Audit trail and evidence generation: Clean, exportable records with integration to Vanta or Drata. Deployment speed: Tools that go live in days, not weeks. Pricing transparency: We noted which vendors hide costs behind sales calls. Shadow IT detection: Orphaned accounts in apps you don't know about are a compliance blind spot. Tools that surface unauthorized application usage scored higher. Best Overall Access Management Tool for SOC 2 Compliance: AccessOwl AccessOwl is an access governance and SaaS management tool built for growing companies that need to automate provisioning, access requests, approvals, access reviews, and Shadow IT detection to meet SOC 2 requirements. It deploys in days, not weeks, and the primary interface is Slack, so your team adopts it without learning another dashboard. What AccessOwl Offers Automated provisioning and deprovisioning across 400+ SaaS applications without requiring SCIM or SAML, which means you're not forced into expensive vendor tiers just to automate account lifecycle management Built-in access review workflows with automatic remediation designed for SOC 2 and ISO 27001 compliance, including time estimates so managers can plan their review sessions Shadow IT discovery through OAuth log analysis from Google Workspace or Microsoft 365, surfacing apps your employees are using that never went through procurement Complete audit trails and evidence collection for compliance reporting, with export capabilities to tools like Vanta HRIS integration for automated onboarding and offboarding workflows triggered by employee start and end dates, removing manual steps from day one Why AccessOwl Works for SOC 2 The access review process is where most small IT teams lose weeks of productivity. With AccessOwl, managers receive Slack notifications, review their direct reports' access in minutes, and any revocations or modifications take effect immediately. There's no lag between identifying a problem and fixing it, which is exactly the kind of gap auditors love to flag. Recurring access reviews should happen at regular intervals: quarterly or annually at minimum, but the remediation shouldn't wait weeks after discovery. For Series A to Series C companies, the integration approach matters. Most provisioning tools rely on SCIM or SAML connections, but those protocols are frequently gated behind enterprise pricing from your SaaS vendors. AccessOwl uses a mix of service accounts, direct API connections, and RPA to automate account lifecycle management across all vendor tiers. You shouldn't have to upgrade to Jira Enterprise just to automate offboarding. Shadow IT detection rounds out the compliance picture. By reading OAuth sign-in logs from your identity provider, AccessOwl automatically surfaces unknown applications and integrates them into offboarding workflows. No orphaned accounts slip through during an audit. If you're the first IT hire and need access governance in place before your next SOC 2 audit window, AccessOwl provides the automation layer to handle it without building a team around the problem. Install the Slack app, connect your HRIS and identity provider, and you're up and running. In this article we broke down how we automate every step of the SOC 2 review process at our own company using AccessOwl. Okta Identity Governance Okta Identity Governance is an add-on governance layer for organizations already invested in the Okta ecosystem. It extends Okta's authentication capabilities into access approvals, reviews, entitlements, and compliance workflows. If your company already runs Okta as its primary identity provider, this feels like the natural next step for SOC 2 access governance. But "natural" and "practical" aren't always the same thing. What They Offer Access request and approval workflows integrated natively with Okta, so governance lives inside the same console your IT team already uses daily Periodic access certification campaigns designed for access controls , with scheduled review cycles and sign-off tracking Entitlement management and separation of duties controls that map user permissions against policy rules Integration with applications already connected to Okta via SCIM and SAML, keeping governance within the existing identity fabric For organizations that have near-complete Okta SSO coverage across their SaaS stack, broad SCIM and SAML integrations already in place, and a dedicated IT team to support longer implementation timelines, Okta Identity Governance can consolidate governance within a single vendor. Where It Falls Short The catch is the prerequisite investment. Okta Identity Governance only works well when companies have already upgraded most SaaS applications to enterprise plans that support SCIM and SAML . Applications outside Okta remain entirely outside the governance workflow, which fragments your access management picture. During rollout, many companies find that a surprising number of their critical apps lack the required integrations unless they spend considerably more on SaaS tier upgrades across their entire stack. This is the "SSO tax" in action, and it compounds fast. If you're a 60-person Series B company running a mix of free-tier, pro, and business-tier SaaS subscriptions, you'll likely hit coverage gaps that leave blind spots in your compliance posture. Those gaps are exactly what auditors will question. Okta Identity Governance makes sense for enterprises already locked into the Okta ecosystem with complete SCIM coverage. For teams that need broad access governance across their actual SaaS environment without first upgrading every application to an enterprise tier, the prerequisites here can become a blocker instead of a shortcut. Corma Corma started as a SaaS spend management and license optimization tool, then added access management features to broaden its market. The core of the product remains finance-driven: cost visibility, license reclamation, and vendor renewal tracking. If your CFO is the one pushing for tooling, Corma might land on the shortlist. But if you're the IT manager trying to pass a SOC 2 audit, the story gets more complicated. What They Offer SaaS spend visibility and license optimization across your application portfolio, giving finance teams a clear picture of where budget is going Shadow IT discovery through a browser extension that tracks which apps employees are actually using, surfacing unauthorized tools before they become audit liabilities Basic access request workflows for routing provisioning tasks through predefined channels Vendor and renewal management to consolidate contract timelines and reduce redundant subscriptions Corma works well for finance-led initiatives where the primary goal is cutting SaaS costs and reclaiming unused licenses, with access governance treated as a secondary benefit. Where It Falls Short The access management layer is thin relative to purpose-built governance tools. Integration coverage skews toward standard identity provider patterns instead of deep, application-specific automation. In practice, provisioning and deprovisioning for many of your critical apps still requires manual intervention. If you're managing 40+ SaaS tools and expecting automated account lifecycle management across all of them, you'll find gaps quickly. Corma excels at telling you how much you're spending and where licenses sit idle. What it doesn't do well is automate the workflows that SOC 2 auditors actually care about: structured approval chains, periodic access reviews with immediate remediation, and clear evidence export. The product solves a spend problem first and treats governance as a bolt-on. For a Series A to Series C IT manager, this ordering matters. If your next audit is in three months and you need access reviews, automated deprovisioning, and a full audit trail, a tool optimized for license reclamation won't close those gaps. Corma is a solid pick when finance is the buyer and cost reduction is the mandate, but less so when your primary driver is passing a SOC 2 audit with minimal manual effort. SailPoint SailPoint is a long-standing name in Identity Governance and Administration (IGA), serving large enterprises in compliance-heavy industries. That reputation is earned, but it comes with a specific buyer profile. What They Offer Access certification campaigns with configurable review cycles, reviewer delegation, and policy-based sign-off workflows designed for SOC 2, ISO 27001, and other regulatory frameworks Role mining and role management capabilities that analyze existing access patterns and suggest role definitions, reducing permission sprawl over time Separation of duties (SoD) policy enforcement to flag and prevent toxic access combinations before they create compliance violations Deep integration with on-premise infrastructure, including Active Directory, mainframes, and legacy systems that cloud-native tools rarely touch AI-driven access recommendations that suggest whether reviewers should approve or revoke specific entitlements based on peer group analysis Where It Falls Short SailPoint was built for thousands of employees with dedicated identity teams. Deployments take months and often require consultants. Pricing isn't public, and contracts start well above what sub-200-person companies budget. For a Series B company with one IT hire who needs to pass a SOC 2 audit next quarter, the timeline and cost don't align with your scale. Why It Works for Large Organizations SailPoint applies AI to detect anomalous access and privilege creep across thousands of identities. The entitlement layer enforces fine-grained permissions across cloud and on-premise systems. Connectors span Active Directory, SAP, Oracle, ServiceNow, mainframes, and hundreds of SaaS apps. SailPoint fits enterprises with mature identity programs, dedicated teams, and six-figure budgets. But for 50 to 200-person companies needing governance before their next audit, the complexity and cost work against you. AccessOwl provides the automation growing companies need without enterprise overhead or six-figure pricing. Entitle Entitle focuses on reducing standing access with temporary, time-bound permissions that expire automatically. Now part of BeyondTrust, it's built around just-in-time (JIT) access. If your security model leans toward least-privilege in cloud infrastructure, Entitle fits. What They Offer Automated provisioning workflows and self-serve access requests across 150+ integrations, letting engineers request what they need without filing tickets Just-in-time access with time-bound permissions that automatically revoke when the window closes, reducing the surface area of standing privileges Integration with on-call tools like PagerDuty for emergency access scenarios, so engineers on rotation can get higher permissions without waiting for manual approvals Cloud infrastructure entitlement management (CIEM) capabilities that map and monitor permissions across AWS, GCP, and Azure environments Where It Falls Short The JIT model assumes security maturity that most Series A to Series C companies haven't reached. When passing a SOC 2 audit is your goal, you need onboarding automation, access reviews with evidence export, and HRIS-tied lifecycle management. For IT managers responsible for 40+ SaaS applications, that gap matters during audit prep. Entitle excels at cloud privilege management. For broader SaaS governance, HRIS-driven automation, and compliance-ready workflows covering your entire stack, AccessOwl delivers without requiring cloud-native security maturity first. ConductorOne ConductorOne is built for companies that have already invested heavily in identity infrastructure. It assumes you've deployed SCIM and SAML across most of your SaaS stack before you start. What They Offer Access request workflows with policy-driven approval chains that route requests based on application sensitivity and organizational hierarchy Automated access certification campaigns designed for SOC 2 and ISO 27001 audit cycles, with reviewer tracking and sign-off workflows Native integration with Okta and other identity providers, pulling entitlement data from connected applications into a centralized governance view Entitlement management for complex permission structures, including visibility into granular roles and group memberships across connected systems Where It Falls Short ConductorOne requires SCIM and SAML, meaning enterprise-tier upgrades are required before governance becomes useful. For a 75-person Series B running mixed subscription tiers, that spend adds up. Implementation takes months because the value depends on the identity provider's coverage. Pricing skews toward the enterprise, with contracts starting above what sub-150-employee companies' budgets allow. If you've built identity foundations and need formal governance, ConductorOne is a good fit. But if you're still solving basics like provisioning and access reviews, you need a tool that doesn't require identity architecture expertise or enterprise pricing across your stack. Feature Comparison Table of Access Management Tools for SOC 2 Compliance Feature AccessOwl Okta Identity Governance Corma SailPoint Entitle ConductorOne Works Without SCIM/SAML Yes No No No No No Automated Access Reviews Yes Yes No Yes No Yes Shadow IT Discovery Yes No Yes No No No Deployment Time Days Months Weeks Months Weeks Months HRIS Integration Yes Yes No Yes No Yes Viable Under 100 Employees Yes No Yes No No No Purpose-Built for Access Governance Yes Yes No Yes No Yes Only AccessOwl automates provisioning without SCIM or SAML, removing the cost of upgrading every app to enterprise tiers. When reviewers flag inappropriate access, AccessOwl revokes it immediately. Every other tool introduces lag. If you're under 100 employees, most tools require dedicated identity teams and six-figure budgets. AccessOwl was purpose-built for access governance at growing companies with lean IT teams. Why AccessOwl Is the Best Access Management Tool for SOC 2 Compliance Every tool on this list solves a piece of the access governance puzzle. But when you're the sole IT hire at a growing company and your SOC 2 audit is approaching, you need something that covers the full scope without forcing you to rebuild your infrastructure first. That's where we fit. AccessOwl connects to 400+ SaaS applications via service accounts, direct APIs, and RPA, helping automated provisioning and deprovisioning regardless of the pricing tier your vendors have you on. No SCIM prerequisite. No SAML tax . No upgrading Jira or Slack to enterprise plans just so your governance tool can talk to them. Access reviews are the other half of the equation. Auditors want evidence that you're periodically reviewing who has access to what and acting on the results. With AccessOwl, managers receive a Slack notification, review their direct reports' access in minutes, and any revocation takes effect immediately. The gap between "we found a problem" and "we fixed it" shrinks to zero, which is exactly the story your auditor wants to hear. Because we pull OAuth sign-in logs from your identity provider, Shadow IT doesn't slip through the cracks during offboarding. Every account gets caught, managed or not. If you're preparing for your first SOC 2 audit and you need access governance running this quarter, not next year, AccessOwl gets you there without the enterprise overhead. Final Thoughts on Access Management for SOC 2 Audits When you're comparing access management tools for SOC 2 , the real question is whether the tool matches your current reality or forces you to build enterprise infrastructure first. Most vendors assume you have unlimited time and budget to upgrade every SaaS app to an enterprise tier, but that's not where Series A to Series C companies actually operate. You need automated provisioning, access reviews with immediate remediation, and Shadow IT detection that works across your actual app portfolio without requiring months of professional services. Check which apps are creating compliance gaps in your environment right now. Your auditor won't care about your resource constraints, so choose a tool that closes the gaps you have today instead of the ones a Fortune 500 company faces. FAQs How do I choose the right access management tool for SOC 2 compliance if I have fewer than 100 employees? Your company size limits your options more than you'd expect. Most tools on the market were built for enterprises and require SCIM/SAML integration, dedicated identity teams, and six-figure budgets. Look for a tool that works without forcing you to upgrade every SaaS app to an enterprise tier first, deploys in days instead of months, and handles the full lifecycle from onboarding through access reviews with immediate remediation. Which SOC 2 access management tool works best if I don't have SCIM or SAML set up across my SaaS stack? AccessOwl is the only tool that automates provisioning and deprovisioning without requiring SCIM or SAML prerequisites. The other options assume you've already upgraded most of your applications to enterprise plans that support those protocols, which adds substantial cost before you even start the governance work. What's the difference between access management tools built for finance teams versus IT teams? Finance-focused tools like Corma focus on spend visibility, license optimization, and vendor management, with access governance layered on as a secondary feature. IT-focused tools like AccessOwl, Okta Identity Governance, and SailPoint treat access governance as the core function, with deeper automation for provisioning, access reviews, and audit evidence. If passing a SOC 2 audit is your primary goal, an IT-focused tool will close more compliance gaps. When should I consider an enterprise-grade tool like SailPoint for SOC 2 instead of a lighter option? SailPoint makes sense when you're managing thousands of employees, running complex hybrid environments with considerable on-premise infrastructure, operating under multiple regulatory frameworks simultaneously, and have a dedicated identity security team with a budget exceeding six figures annually. If you're a sub-200-person company with one IT hire, the implementation timeline and cost structure work against you. How is an access management tool like AccessOwl different from Vanta or Drata? Vanta and Drata are broad compliance platforms. They do monitor your controls, flag gaps, and collect evidence for your SOC 2 audit, but they don't provision accounts, run the access reviews, or revoke access for you. AccessOwl does. It routes access reviews to the right reviewer, executes the remediation action with one click, and exports clean evidence. Most compliant teams will layer AccessOwl on top of a platform like Vanta or Drata to further automate manual processes.

title: Superwall acquires Tangent and raises $7.5M
summary: Superwall has raised $7.5M and acquired Tangent, the monetization consultancy founded by Vahe Baghdasaryan. Tangent still works with any subscription app, whether or not you use Superwall.
body_text: Tangent is now a Superwall company Today we're announcing that Superwall has acquired Tangent. Tangent is the best monetization consultancy in the business, the team behind some of the highest-converting subscription screens on the App Store. Going forward, they operate as Tangent, a Superwall company. If you haven't come across them, Tangent designs paywalls, runs pricing and offer experiments, and ships the kind of monetization work most teams never get to because it sits behind an engineering queue. Tangent has launched more than 5,000 experiments and designed over 20,000 paywalls across more than 100 subscription apps, work it credits with more than $50M in added revenue, and its clients see their average ARPU rise 30 to 40% within three months. Their customers include Cal AI , ElevenLabs , Elevate , Pixelcut , Lose It , Praktika , WeWard , Stardust , Hallow , NGL , ReciMe , and Fig . Meet Vahe Tangent started as a one-person operation called Paywalls Design. Vahe Baghdasaryan would design a paywall for a few hundred dollars, post the results on X, and let the work speak for itself. That pipeline turned into a seven-figure consultancy with more than 20 people, and Inc. wrote up how he built it almost entirely through Twitter. Vahe knows monetization from the inside. He previously worked on monetization strategy at Flo, and he is a regular speaker on subscription growth at conferences like MAU Vegas, Business of Apps, and RAGA. Superwall raises $7.5M and acquires Tangent There's a second piece of news here. Superwall has raised $7.5M to date, from Nico Wittenborn's Adjacent and Acurio , with participation from Y Combinator and FJ Labs. We haven't made a point of announcing our funding before. It was never where our focus went, but enough people ask that it felt worth sharing. We were profitable before this acquisition, and we're more profitable now. The money isn't there to keep the lights on, it's there to push. We're investing heavily in both our product and our services. Business as usual: Tangent works with anyone Here is the most important part for Tangent's clients: nothing about how Tangent works is changing. Tangent works with any subscription app, whether or not you use Superwall. If you run your paywalls in RevenueCat, Helium, or Adapty, Tangent will build and test them there. If you just want the designs, they will hand you the Figma files and let your team take it from there. The tool you monetize on is your choice, and it always will be. Same team, same clients, same work. The acquisition gives Tangent more resources to do it, not a reason to narrow who they do it for. Why Superwall and Tangent Superwall exists so growth teams can test anything, fast, without shipping a build. Tangent is the team that knows exactly what to test and how to read the results. Design and experimentation on one side, the tooling to run it without an engineering queue on the other. The two fit together. We think of product and services as moats for each other. Superwall's product makes Tangent's work faster and sharper, and Tangent's work in the field teaches us exactly what to build next. Together, Tangent and Superwall can serve customers better than either could alone. For Superwall customers, this means you can now bring in Tangent to design and run your paywall experiments end to end, as a fully managed service if you want it. For everyone else, Tangent is exactly what it was yesterday. If you want to work with Tangent, whatever stack you are on, take a look at Superwall Services or book a free audit with Vahe . FAQ Does the acquisition change who Tangent works with? No. Tangent works with any subscription app, whether or not you use Superwall. That includes teams on RevenueCat, Helium, and Adapty, or teams that just want the paywall designs as Figma files. Do I need to use Superwall to work with Tangent? No. The monetization tool you use is your choice. Tangent will build and test paywalls on whatever stack you already run, and hand off designs if that is all you need. What is Tangent? Tangent is a monetization consultancy founded by Vahe Baghdasaryan. It designs paywalls, runs pricing and offer tests, and manages monetization experiments for subscription apps. Tangent has launched more than 5,000 experiments and designed over 20,000 paywalls, and its clients see their average ARPU rise 30 to 40% within three months. Its customers include Cal AI, ElevenLabs, Elevate, Hallow, NGL, and ReciMe. Who is Vahe Baghdasaryan? Vahe is the founder of Tangent. He previously worked on monetization strategy at Flo and is a regular speaker on subscription growth at conferences like MAU Vegas, Business of Apps, and RAGA. How much has Superwall raised, and from whom? Superwall has raised $7.5M to date, from Nico Wittenborn's Adjacent and Acurio, with participation from Y Combinator and FJ Labs. Superwall hasn't typically announced its funding and is sharing it now, alongside the Tangent acquisition, because people ask. What does the acquisition mean for Superwall customers? Superwall customers can now bring in Tangent to design and run paywall experiments end to end, as a fully managed service if they want it. Tangent's expertise pairs with Superwall's ability to test paywalls without shipping an app release. How do I work with Tangent? You can book a free audit with Vahe at cal.com/bvahe/30min, whatever monetization stack you use.

title: Tech Trends 2025 by Wipro: Driving Enterprise Innovation with Emerging Tech
summary: Emerging Technologies 2025 by Wipro shows how Agentic AI, Autonomous Machines, and Blockchain enhance enterprise performance and growth
body_text: Wipro’s Tech Trends for 2025 Wipro’s Tech Trends for 2025 report highlights key technology trends that are poised to transform industries and shape the future of enterprises. As technology increasingly mirrors human behaviour, with disruptive scale and speed, enterprises are set to accelerate the integration of AI and other advanced technologies to unlock significant business value. A global team of experts in Wipro Lab45 focuses on incubating emerging tech and client-centric innovations. This report draws on insights from clients, partners, startups, academia, and studies by Wipro Lab45 Research. 1. The Emergence of Agentic Enterprises Imagine a future where AI Agents autonomously make decisions and collaborate to achieve business goals once they are assigned roles and provided with the business context. In 2025, enterprises will reimagine business processes and value streams with AI Agents, while taking into consideration the practical and ethical challenges. In the coming years, AI Agents will generate new revenue streams, innovate business processes across industries, boosting profitability, operational efficiency, and customer experience. Humans will increasingly take on roles where they set up agentic teams, plan agentic workflows, and validate work done by AI Agents. 2. The Rise of Autonomous Machines The idea of Software Defined capabilities, which originated with cloud technology, has now evolved across various machines like vehicles and robots. In 2025, software defined machines will be powered by AI & ML and make informed decisions. We will witness an increase in autonomous machines with over-the-air (OTA) updates. Autonomous industrial robots will proliferate, and Software Defined Medical Devices will evolve towards autonomous preventive maintenance and self-healing with minimal human intervention and down time. Telecom and Network Equipment Providers will embark on the maturity roadmap for Autonomous Networks providing bandwidth on demand. 3. The Maturing of Industry Cloud AI-powered industry cloud solutions will mature. Industry Cloud Platforms will feature pre-built Industry AI models and tools optimized for common industry-specific needs. These platforms will also bring crucial capabilities like the integration of industry-relevant data sources, data privacy, security, and compliance. We will see increased collaboration and governance by industry-tech consortiums to unlock value from data across value networks with AI. 4. Smart World Interactions The usage of extended reality (XR) will increase. In this evolving landscape, multimodal AI will seamlessly integrate into real-world human interactions and navigation. Technology will become more intuitive and responsive to human needs including security and privacy, offering enterprises new opportunities to elevate customer experiences and empower employees. For example, spatial computing will augment customer service, buyer experiences, traveler experiences, patient-provider interactions, and remote work. XR and AI powered solutions for inspection and preventive maintenance will impact safety and environmental protection in addition to operational efficiency. 5. The Democratization of Data Augmented Analytics will enable citizen users to gain access to intelligent insights from ready-to-use data visualizations for faster and informed decision making. Data marketplaces will grow across industries and industry ecosystems to unlock new revenue streams. Enterprises will navigate the unstoppable wave of data democratization. They will need to address the widespread concerns associated with AI bias, copyright protection, data privacy, and data security. ROI from AI will demand superior data quality with industry and business context. 6. Acceleration in Blockchain Blockchain has re-emerged as a robust and transformative technology, leading to decentralised internet. Blockchain infrastructure is expected to complement digital commerce infrastructure as people globally transact financially on the internet. Many countries have set up CBDC (Central Bank Digital Currencies) and RLN (Regulated Liability Networks), with many more planning to do so. While financial institutions lead the way, almost all industries will enjoy the benefits of traceability, increased security, inbuilt trust, and transparency among members. We will see an acceleration in adoption in 2025 as both the technology and regulations mature to mitigate impediments to adoption to realise the undisputed benefits of the blockchain. 7. Preparing for Quantum Computing Enterprises will gear up for the Quantum Era with Quantum Computing as a Service (QCaaS). The immediate priority for global enterprises will be to prepare for post-quantum cryptography. Biopharma and chemical industries will be early adopters of Quantum Computing with applications in molecular modeling, predictive analytics, and drug design. Enterprises will also need to consider the regulatory guidelines & ethical practices evolving around this cutting edge technology. 8. Cyber Resilience With disruptive technologies like AI and Quantum computing enterprises will redefine cyber resilience. Enterprises will use AI-powered cybersecurity solutions for protection from AI-based risks. Real-time analysis, pattern recognition, and predictive defence capabilities will combat new and sophisticated cyber threats such as deepfakes, social engineering, cyber-attacks, data poisoning, and AI model theft. 9. Sustainable Tech Sustainability is of strategic importance to global enterprises. The focus will be on using AI and non-AI systems to optimize resource usage, reduce waste, and improve energy efficiency. AI will augment existing solutions in telemetry and visual analytics for sustainability. However, the AI-Tech remains resource intensive. Energy consumption by AI and the proliferation of data centres are major concerns, and efforts are underway to make the AI stack more sustainable from silicon to software. 2025 promises to be a year of high-velocity technology disruptions, offering new opportunities and presenting unprecedented challenges. The future belongs to enterprises that embrace technology and disruption, responding swiftly by collaborating with partners like Wipro to innovate. About the Authors Hitarshi Meenketu Buch Hitarshi has over 2 decades of experience in IT architecture, consulting, design and implementation using blockchain, API, SOA, BPM and Java/J2EE technologies. In his current role, as a Chief Architect in the office of CTO, he is responsible for Wipro DICE ID platform as well as formulating strategy and incubating emerging technologies. Varun Dube Varun Dube is the Head of Tech Strategy at Wipro. He is a seasoned technology consultant, advising CXOs on transformative business outcomes. With a deep understanding of emerging technologies and their potential to disrupt industries, Varun drives innovation and digital transformation for Wipro clients . His expertise in crafting and executing technology strategies, combined with his focus on emerging tech and co-innovation, helps organizations achieve sustainable growth and competitive advantage. Sandhya Arun Sandhya Arun is the Chief Technology Officer at Wipro. She has led key initiatives in digital transformation and AI, supporting client success and business growth. Sandhya has extensively published and presented her insights on experience design, digital transformation, and artificial intelligence in various industry and expert fora. Sandhya emphasizes leveraging emerging technologies for societal benefit and leads the Women in Tech initiative. Her 30-year career spans roles in Technology Consulting, Cloud and Engineering Transformation, Digital Commerce and Marketing, and Human-Centric Design.
